title: Using the on-screen calculator and the note board
blurb: Key Part A calculations on a Standard calculator in a safe order, using the note board to hold the formula and full values.
question: You need 420 mg from a liquid labelled 120 mg/5 mL. Which keys on a Standard calculator give the volume, and what is it?

teach.h: A Standard calculator and a note board
teach.body: Part A gives you an on-screen calculator; the Pearson practice test offers Standard mode only, so there are no scientific functions to lean on. You also get an erasable note board and marker, but writing on it before the tutorial ends counts as "brain dumping". Plain English: write the formula first, then key one clear chain of steps.

head: Task
Keys
Display
teach.caption: Convert units before keying: 0.25 mg = 250 micrograms.

teach.h: Worked example: Kofi on a mental health ward
teach.body: Kofi, 45, is prescribed amitriptyline 35 mg; the oral solution is 25 mg/5 mL. On the note board: 35 ÷ 25 × 5. Keys: 35 ÷ 25 = 1.4, × 5 = 7. Volume = 7 mL. Sense-check: 35 mg is a little more than 25 mg, so a little more than 5 mL fits.

Standard mode is not a scientific calculator, so do not rely on brackets or try to key a whole formula in one go. Work the part that would be in brackets first and press =. For 500 mL over 2 hours 40 minutes: 40 ÷ 60 = 0.666…, + 2 = 2.666…; note that on the board, then 500 ÷ 2.666… = 187.5. Keep the full value rather than retyping a rounded one.

teach.text: Three keying slips: putting the fraction upside down (have ÷ want), dividing by the stock volume instead of multiplying, and typing hours-and-minutes as a decimal (2 h 45 min is 2.75, not 2.45). Write the formula on the note board before touching the keys.

items: Write the formula on the note board first.
Convert units before you key anything.
Do not rely on brackets: work the inner step first and press =.
Copy the full display; round only at the end.

summary: You can now plan a calculation on the note board and key it on a Standard calculator one step at a time, converting units first. You can also avoid the classic keying slips: inverted fractions, ÷ for ×, and minutes typed as decimals.

A.q: You have a prescription for 420 mg. The bottle label reads 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: Keyed the fraction upside down (have ÷ want).

A.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 1500 mL, IV, over 12 hours. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
You have a prescription for 0.5 mg. The tablets contain 250 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.0: Divided without converting mg to micrograms.
whyNot.3: Converted mg to micrograms with × 100 instead of × 1000.

B.q: A person weighing 76 kg is prescribed 1.5 mg/kg of a medicine. The vial label reads 50 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 500 mL, IV, over 3 hours 20 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

whyNot.3: Divided by 200 minutes: that is mL per minute.

B.q: A child weighing 14 kg is prescribed 15 micrograms/kg of a medicine. The ampoule label reads 500 micrograms in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

C.q: You have a prescription for 1.2 g. The oral suspension label reads 500 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Keyed 1.2 without converting g to mg.

C.q: A person is prescribed 3 mg per hour of a medicine by intravenous infusion. The syringe contains 100 mg in 50 mL. At what rate should the pump be set?
C.why: Concentration = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 mg/mL. Rate = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 mL per hour.

whyNot.0: Multiplied by the concentration instead of dividing.

C.q: You have a prescription for 750 mg three times a day for 7 days. The tablets contain 250 mg each. How many tablets are needed for the whole course?
C.why: 750 ÷ 250 = 3 tablets per dose. × 3 doses × 7 days = 63 tablets.

whyNot.0: Counted one tablet per dose; each dose is 3 tablets.

reteach.title: Formula first, keys second
reteach.question: 360 mg is prescribed from 120 mg/5 mL. Which keys give the volume?

blocks.h: Say it, write it, key it
blocks.body: Want ÷ have × volume. Written: 360 ÷ 120 × 5. Keyed: 360 ÷ 120 = 3, then × 5 = 15 mL.

blocks.text: 0.6 mL is a tiny volume for a dose three times the stock strength: the sense-check catches the slip.

explain.body: Key the wanted dose first, divide by the stock strength, then multiply by the stock volume.

test.q: You have a prescription for 35 mg. The oral solution label reads 25 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

explain.body: Put the prescription and the label in the same unit first.

test.q: You have a prescription for 0.15 mg. The tablets contain 50 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.1: Divided without converting mg to micrograms.

explain.body: Minutes ÷ 60, then add the whole hours: 7 h 30 min = 7.5 h.

test.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 7 hours 30 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
test.why: 7 hours 30 minutes = 7.5 hours. 1000 ÷ 7.5 = 133.33..., so 133 mL per hour.

whyNot.2: Divided by minutes: that is mL per minute.

explain.body: Do not retype a rounded middle value; keep the chain going on the calculator.

test.q: You have a prescription for 50 mg. The ampoule label reads 30 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
